SUMMARY
In the 2026 Primary Election, voters showed
moderate support of the ballot measures
presented to them – a significant decline from
the generally good support achieved during the
2024 Primary Election with approval rates of
62.9% and 72.2%, respectively. Although the
2024 Primary contained one statewide GO
bond measure, the overall number of local
ballot measures presented to voters was the
same (89) for both the 2024 and 2026 Primary
Elections.
In both Primaries, measures for Education
purposes comprised the highest concentration
of ballot measures: 57.8% in 2024 and 48.3%
in 2026. However, there was an overall
decrease of 17.3% in the number of Education
measures with 52 presented in 2024 versus
43 in 2026. When compared by passage rates,
2024 had a higher passage rate for education
measures (65.4%) than those presented in
2026 (60.5%).
Ballot measures for both Capital Improvements
and Public Works and General Government
increased significantly from 2024 to 2026 at
rates of 160% (5 to 13) and 71.4% (14 to 24)
respectively. However, the passage rate for
Capital Improvements and Public Works at
80% and 76.9% in 2024 and 2026 Primaries
differed greatly from the outcome for General
Government measures which decreased from
92.9% in 2024 to 66.7% in 2026. Voter
support was weak overall in 2026 for Public
Safety measures (44.4%) compared to
relatively good support in 2024 (76.9%).

INTRODUCTION
Constitutional and statutory provisions require voters
to authorize general obligation (GO) bonds issued by
state and local governments. For bonds issued by the
state, the authorization must be made through a
statewide election. Local bonds must be approved by
voters within the jurisdiction authorizing the bond.
The state and local governments must also seek voter
approval for levies of certain revenue exactions and
taxes. For both state and local measures, the voter
approval threshold depends on the type and purpose
of the bond or tax (see Figure 1).
The California Debt and Investment Advisory
Commission (CDIAC) publishes a statistical summary
and review of bond and tax measures appearing on
state and local ballots. This report, the 44th in the
series, summarizes the results of local bond and
tax measures considered by voters during local
elections held in 2025 and includes an appendix
summarizing the measures by county. A summary of
each measure from 1986 through 2025 is also
available through DebtWatch.

SUMMARY
Overall, voters were slightly more supportive of the
local bond and tax measures in the 2023 local
elections (73.3%) than the 2025 local elections
(63.0%). The number of measures requiring a
majority to pass jumped from 2 in 2023 to 11 in
2025, eight of which were for sales tax increases
primarily for General Government purposes and three
of which were special taxes placed on the ballot by
citizen initiative requiring only a simple majority for
passage instead of two-thirds. The 2023 elections
had one combined parcel tax and special tax bond
that did not pass whereas in 2025 there were two,
both of which passed. In 2023, Public Health and
Safety measures comprised 46.7% of all ballot
measures, however in the 2025 local elections,
measures proposed for that purpose dropped to
18.5%. Ballot measures for General Government and
Capital Improvements and Public Works purposes
totaled 7 tax measures each or 25.9% of the 2025
total. In both elections, the passage rate for the
region of Los Angeles remained at 100%. The
passage rate of special tax measures was lower in
2025 (47.1%), then in 2023 (76.0%).

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

# The Unintended Consequences of Measure ULA
Report
Michael Manville | Mott Smith
April 2025
We present evidence suggesting that Measure ULA has reduced higher-end real estate transactions in Los Angeles.
Since Measure ULA was enacted, the odds of a Los Angeles property selling at a price above its tax threshold have fallen by as much as 50%.
In raw terms, this sharp decline occurred across all types of properties, but our strongest evidence suggests it was particularly pronounced for non-single family transactions, which fell by 30-50%.
Together the evidence suggests that Measure ULA is neither a true “Mansion Tax,” nor a tax that falls solely on unearned property wealth.
The tax does fall on mansions, but it also impedes the trade in commercial, industrial and multifamily property.
In doing so it jeopardizes L.A.’s ability to build new housing, revitalize struggling commercial and industrial properties, and raise property tax revenue.
All these processes rely on property turnover, and in particular the turnover of higher-priced, non-single family parcels.
A tax that reduces this turnover will undermine property tax revenues inside and outside L.A., obstruct local and regional housing production, and slow local revitalization efforts.
Thus while Measure ULA has generated visible, substantial and much-needed revenues for affordable housing in Los Angeles, it has also, less visibly, had consequences that reduce both housing affordability and fiscal health.

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects
***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.
The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

**Evaluating election data**

I’m looking at the recent data from the elections in 2025 and 2026, focusing on voter-led special taxes. In the 2025 local elections, 3 out of 14 special taxes passed with a majority (66.7%), while in 2026, out of 7 citizen special taxes, 4 were approved (57.1%). It’s interesting to note that if all 35 special taxes had only needed a simple majority, they would have had an 88.6% pass rate. I'll dig deeper into the specifics of Prop43.**Inspecting election data**

I need to look closely at the appendices for percentages related to the 2026 elections. Out of the 7 measures, four passed by a majority—could all of these have achieved at least 2/3? It seems possible that some were citizen initiatives. I'm also thinking about specific examples from 2025, like the health care parcel tax that passed with 64.77% but would have failed under Prop43. This data really shows how thresholds affect specific services, and I should check the details in the 2026 table.**Analyzing voter-led taxes**

Looking at the data from 2025, I see that 2 out of 3 voter-led special taxes passed with a simple majority. However, if a 2/3 threshold had been required, would they have succeeded? For example, the healthcare district initiative passed with 64.77%, which is just below the 2/3 mark and would have failed under those stricter requirements. This shows how the voting threshold can significantly impact outcomes for voter initiatives.**Evaluating tax implications**

I'm considering whether lowering taxes would benefit most households. Tax savings can be spread out among many, but the costs of services may end up concentrated among users. It's tricky because property tax interacts with services. There's also a proposition that acts as a barrier for local taxes, letting voters reject taxes. For those who think voters tend to overspend, a supermajority requirement can help prevent a minority from imposing costs on others. Taxation impacts everyone, especially the minority.**Analyzing local tax implications**

I’m considering how common property tax increases, like special taxes, could disproportionately impact homeowners and retirees. The 2/3 requirement aims for broader support, especially since taxing affects everyone, including nonvoters like businesses and visitors, and may last indefinitely. It prevents private interests from influencing tax votes. A majority can lead to unfair taxes, so the 2/3 rule serves as a safeguard. I should investigate if Prop 13 special taxes always needed this 2/3 majority. Are there underlying legal reasons for its existence?**Exploring local government tax initiatives**

I’m pondering how local government initiatives work. It seems direct tax initiatives historically need only a simple majority unless stated otherwise. The Upland case appears to have settled the issue legally, meaning Prop 43 is more of a policy choice than a correction. While the anti-tax narrative about “special interests” could be true, initiative sponsors can still be subject to public voting and disclosure. Supermajority requirements can serve as a safeguard, but they present a significant hurdle. Do voters overlook how special districts impact tax classification?**Evaluating impacts of special districts**

I’m thinking about how special districts, which exceed 2,000 in the state, affect various public services like schools and fire districts. All proposed taxes require a 2/3 vote, while recent examples show that in the 2026 local tax primary, four out of seven citizen-initiated special taxes passed with only 57.1%. If the 2/3 rule was applied, some might have failed, including a health district tax that wouldn’t pass under this requirement. Prop 43 doesn’t impact existing taxes, but future extensions will necessitate the supermajority.**Researching arguments and effects**

I think “do extensive research” could involve looking at the positions of various arguments and their real-world effects. But we’ve already done a lot of work with searches on official texts and analyses, like LAO, campaign finance for 2025/2026, CDIAC, and PPIC. It feels like we’ve done enough to cover the essentials. I want to keep the final results focused and minimal while considering all angles.

**Evaluating election data**

I’m looking at the recent data from the elections in 2025 and 2026, focusing on voter-led special taxes. In the 2025 local elections, 3 out of 14 special taxes passed with a majority (66.7%), while in 2026, out of 7 citizen special taxes, 4 were approved (57.1%). It’s interesting to note that if all 35 special taxes had only needed a simple majority, they would have had an 88.6% pass rate. I'll dig deeper into the specifics of Prop43.**Inspecting election data**

I need to look closely at the appendices for percentages related to the 2026 elections. Out of the 7 measures, four passed by a majority—could all of these have achieved at least 2/3? It seems possible that some were citizen initiatives. I'm also thinking about specific examples from 2025, like the health care parcel tax that passed with 64.77% but would have failed under Prop43. This data really shows how thresholds affect specific services, and I should check the details in the 2026 table.**Analyzing voter-led taxes**

Looking at the data from 2025, I see that 2 out of 3 voter-led special taxes passed with a simple majority. However, if a 2/3 threshold had been required, would they have succeeded? For example, the healthcare district initiative passed with 64.77%, which is just below the 2/3 mark and would have failed under those stricter requirements. This shows how the voting threshold can significantly impact outcomes for voter initiatives.**Evaluating tax implications**

I'm considering whether lowering taxes would benefit most households. Tax savings can be spread out among many, but the costs of services may end up concentrated among users. It's tricky because property tax interacts with services. There's also a proposition that acts as a barrier for local taxes, letting voters reject taxes. For those who think voters tend to overspend, a supermajority requirement can help prevent a minority from imposing costs on others. Taxation impacts everyone, especially the minority.**Analyzing local tax implications**

I’m considering how common property tax increases, like special taxes, could disproportionately impact homeowners and retirees. The 2/3 requirement aims for broader support, especially since taxing affects everyone, including nonvoters like businesses and visitors, and may last indefinitely. It prevents private interests from influencing tax votes. A majority can lead to unfair taxes, so the 2/3 rule serves as a safeguard. I should investigate if Prop 13 special taxes always needed this 2/3 majority. Are there underlying legal reasons for its existence?**Exploring local government tax initiatives**

I’m pondering how local government initiatives work. It seems direct tax initiatives historically need only a simple majority unless stated otherwise. The Upland case appears to have settled the issue legally, meaning Prop 43 is more of a policy choice than a correction. While the anti-tax narrative about “special interests” could be true, initiative sponsors can still be subject to public voting and disclosure. Supermajority requirements can serve as a safeguard, but they present a significant hurdle. Do voters overlook how special districts impact tax classification?**Evaluating impacts of special districts**

I’m thinking about how special districts, which exceed 2,000 in the state, affect various public services like schools and fire districts. All proposed taxes require a 2/3 vote, while recent examples show that in the 2026 local tax primary, four out of seven citizen-initiated special taxes passed with only 57.1%. If the 2/3 rule was applied, some might have failed, including a health district tax that wouldn’t pass under this requirement. Prop 43 doesn’t impact existing taxes, but future extensions will necessitate the supermajority.**Researching arguments and effects**

I think “do extensive research” could involve looking at the positions of various arguments and their real-world effects. But we’ve already done a lot of work with searches on official texts and analyses, like LAO, campaign finance for 2025/2026, CDIAC, and PPIC. It feels like we’ve done enough to cover the essentials. I want to keep the final results focused and minimal while considering all angles.

**Evaluating election data**

I’m looking at the recent data from the elections in 2025 and 2026, focusing on voter-led special taxes. In the 2025 local elections, 3 out of 14 special taxes passed with a majority (66.7%), while in 2026, out of 7 citizen special taxes, 4 were approved (57.1%). It’s interesting to note that if all 35 special taxes had only needed a simple majority, they would have had an 88.6% pass rate. I'll dig deeper into the specifics of Prop43.**Inspecting election data**

I need to look closely at the appendices for percentages related to the 2026 elections. Out of the 7 measures, four passed by a majority—could all of these have achieved at least 2/3? It seems possible that some were citizen initiatives. I'm also thinking about specific examples from 2025, like the health care parcel tax that passed with 64.77% but would have failed under Prop43. This data really shows how thresholds affect specific services, and I should check the details in the 2026 table.**Analyzing voter-led taxes**

Looking at the data from 2025, I see that 2 out of 3 voter-led special taxes passed with a simple majority. However, if a 2/3 threshold had been required, would they have succeeded? For example, the healthcare district initiative passed with 64.77%, which is just below the 2/3 mark and would have failed under those stricter requirements. This shows how the voting threshold can significantly impact outcomes for voter initiatives.**Evaluating tax implications**

I'm considering whether lowering taxes would benefit most households. Tax savings can be spread out among many, but the costs of services may end up concentrated among users. It's tricky because property tax interacts with services. There's also a proposition that acts as a barrier for local taxes, letting voters reject taxes. For those who think voters tend to overspend, a supermajority requirement can help prevent a minority from imposing costs on others. Taxation impacts everyone, especially the minority.**Analyzing local tax implications**

I’m considering how common property tax increases, like special taxes, could disproportionately impact homeowners and retirees. The 2/3 requirement aims for broader support, especially since taxing affects everyone, including nonvoters like businesses and visitors, and may last indefinitely. It prevents private interests from influencing tax votes. A majority can lead to unfair taxes, so the 2/3 rule serves as a safeguard. I should investigate if Prop 13 special taxes always needed this 2/3 majority. Are there underlying legal reasons for its existence?**Exploring local government tax initiatives**

I’m pondering how local government initiatives work. It seems direct tax initiatives historically need only a simple majority unless stated otherwise. The Upland case appears to have settled the issue legally, meaning Prop 43 is more of a policy choice than a correction. While the anti-tax narrative about “special interests” could be true, initiative sponsors can still be subject to public voting and disclosure. Supermajority requirements can serve as a safeguard, but they present a significant hurdle. Do voters overlook how special districts impact tax classification?**Evaluating impacts of special districts**

I’m thinking about how special districts, which exceed 2,000 in the state, affect various public services like schools and fire districts. All proposed taxes require a 2/3 vote, while recent examples show that in the 2026 local tax primary, four out of seven citizen-initiated special taxes passed with only 57.1%. If the 2/3 rule was applied, some might have failed, including a health district tax that wouldn’t pass under this requirement. Prop 43 doesn’t impact existing taxes, but future extensions will necessitate the supermajority.**Researching arguments and effects**

I think “do extensive research” could involve looking at the positions of various arguments and their real-world effects. But we’ve already done a lot of work with searches on official texts and analyses, like LAO, campaign finance for 2025/2026, CDIAC, and PPIC. It feels like we’ve done enough to cover the essentials. I want to keep the final results focused and minimal while considering all angles.
